### Prerequisites the catalog imposes on the machinery

- `validate_output` needs `enum` (provenance, action state, region kind, section names) and `maxLength` before the first row using them merges; extend it with tests. Input unions such as the facets of `object_place` are the decoder's job, not the schema validator's.
- Neither adapter needs new loading machinery. The projection tests need to record definition bytes per adapter, and the live regression needs to record input and cached tokens per request, so the deferral decision is evidence-based.
- The coordinator needs [grouped approvals](#grouped-approvals) and the `planId` field on every mutation.
- Three owners are trapped in presentation code and need a product-neutral seam first: mapping and readiness logic in `SelectMachineDialog` for `preflight_check`; plane and circle detection in the Measure gizmo for `object_analyze`; offscreen preview rendering for `view_render` preview mode. Import and open need the dialog choices (`loadProjectSettings`, `unitConversion`, `oversized`) reachable without the dialogs, the same hazard class as the settings normalizer.
- The JusPrin stores for intent, plan, regions, confirmed facts, and monitoring policy do not exist yet; rules under [JusPrin-owned project state](#jusprin-owned-project-state).
- The image projections under [Image results](#image-results) in both adapters before `project_attachment_read`, `view_render`, or `printer_camera_snapshot` ships.
- The Tier 1 security review under [Proportional security growth](#proportional-security-growth).

### Evals that gate delivery

1. Open a one-object STL, state "decorative, front face visible, under five hours, PLA", and reach a sent job with no manual setting edits. Needs `core`, `project`, `setup`, `geometry`, `output`. Its transcript is also the first call log for consolidation: any two tools always called together are candidates to merge.
2. A model with a precision hole and a support-heavy overhang: find the hole, annotate it as protected, show that supports no longer enter it after re-slicing, and place the seam on a hidden face. Needs `regions` and `check`.
3. Stringing reported on a Bambu printer: list tests, generate a temperature tower, read the user's photo, propose a filament temperature, preview and apply it with `persistAs`. Needs `calibration` and the filament scope.
4. Concurrent edit: the user changes a setting in the GUI while an external agent has a pending apply. The apply fails as stale and the agent recovers with one preview and one apply. Every toolset.
5. Load measurement: the live regression reports, per request, definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for the full catalog, and the transcript is reviewed for wrong-tool selections. These numbers decide whether deferral is adopted.

## Process-settings tools: contract and hazards

The settings tools are the reference implementation of this guide. What
follows is the part of their design that stays true after the work is done;
the implementation handoff that produced it is retired. Re-read this section
before expanding the write allowlist or adding a tool that changes a preset.

### Standing decisions

1. Settings are data: four generic tools over searchable records, never one
   tool per setting.
2. Only the active FFF process preset's edited configuration is in scope. No
### The normalizer can open dialogs and rewrite values

`update_print_fff_config` and `toggle_print_fff_options` in
`src/slic3r/GUI/ConfigManipulation.cpp` run inside `TabPrint::update()` after
every batch and evaluate every rule against the whole post-batch config, not
only the changed keys. Some rules open a modal dialog and then rewrite a
value; others rewrite silently. A modal opened from inside a tool execution
blocks the GUI thread while the request waits, and a silent rewrite makes the
result lie unless it is reported.

Two rules follow. Preview evaluates the same rule set against a clone, using
the printer preset and filament count the adapter can read, so a rule that
fires because of a pre-existing value is reported too. Dialog rules are
blocking issues; silent rules are warnings that name the dependent key and
its predicted value (`normalized_dependency`), and apply lists the actual
rewrite under `normalized`. Preview reuses Orca's `ConfigManipulation` on the
clone with no presentation callbacks rather than copying its option tables.

Rules reachable through the current allowlist, as audited when the tools
were built. Line numbers drift; search for the condition text.

| Rule in Orca | Reached by | Effect | Preview must |
|---|---|---|---|
| `layer_height` at or below epsilon | `layer_height` | modal, reset to 0.2 | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the minimum |
| `layer_height` above the printer's `max_layer_height` when that exceeds 0.2 | `layer_height` | modal, clamp | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the printer's maximum |
| `seam_slope_type` not `None` and absolute `seam_slope_start_height` at or above `layer_height` | lowering `layer_height` | modal, start height reset to 0 | refuse with `incompatible_settings`; evaluate percent values through `get_abs_value`, 100% or above also trips it |
| `spiral_mode` on and not all of `wall_loops` 1, `top_shell_layers` 0, `sparse_infill_density` 0 | those three keys | yes/no dialog, several keys rewritten either way | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `spiral_mode` |
| `sparse_infill_pattern` without multiline support while `fill_multiline` is above 1 | `sparse_infill_pattern` | silent: `fill_multiline` reset to 1 | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
| support-gap rounding block | none; it is inside `#if 0` | inactive | do not predict a change that does not happen |

Every active dialog predicate must be checked, including pre-existing
invalid ironing spacing, first-layer height, XY and elephant-foot
compensation, alternate-extra-wall, infill-lock depth, and fuzzy-skin
settings; spiral mode also checks support, enforced support layers, thin
walls, overhang reversal, timelapse, and wrapping detection. The real-adapter
test asserts that no top-level dialog appears during apply for any
allowlisted key under every row above, and that every predicted silent
rewrite appears in the result with its actual value. A rule found later that
a tool can trigger is a defect in the preview, not accepted behavior. Adding
a key to the allowlist means re-reading both functions for every place that
key is read and extending this table.

### Approval binds the values the user saw

Apply is previewed three times. The client previews and sees before and
after values. At proposal time the coordinator previews again on the GUI
thread, so an invalid patch fails at once without an approval card, and
stores that result as the confirmed set the user approves; the approval
title names the keys from it. At execution the adapter previews a third time
against the then-current config and compares every before value against the
confirmed set: a moved value is `stale_workspace`, a blocking issue is
`invalid_settings`, and neither mutates. Client-supplied values are never
trusted as before values. Where Orca normalized a value differently from the
preview, the actual value is returned and the key is listed under
`normalized`; the mutation happened, so that is a success with an honest
report.

### Registry facts worth knowing

- `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute` dispatches on `ToolHandler` with
  explicit blocks; add a block per tool, not a generic dispatch table.
- `kInvalidatingReasons` is one global mask and includes `Settings`, so any
  pending proposal fails with `stale_revision` when the user edits a setting
  in the GUI. A per-tool mask is a later refinement if evals show friction.
- `ToolRegistry::validate_output` accepts a closed schema vocabulary: `type`,
  `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `minimum`,
  `maxItems`. Any other keyword throws; extend the validator with a test
  before using a new keyword.
- Codex CLI needs `tool_timeout_sec` raised above its 60-second default for
  approval-gated calls.

### Upstream seams the tool system owns

Two added lines in `src/CMakeLists.txt`, eight in
`src/dev-utils/platform/unix/build_linux_image.sh.in`, and one additive
`notify_project_state_changed(ProjectStateChangeReason::Settings)` call at
the end of `Plater::on_config_change`. `Plater.cpp` is the fork's busiest
file; when that function changes upstream, the natural resolution is "keep
both". No line in `Tab.cpp`, `ConfigManipulation.cpp`, or `PrintConfig.cpp`
changes; the normalizer hazards are handled by refusing the inputs in
fork-owned code.

## Proportional security growth

Keep the local baseline: automatic startup with the JusPrin Agent panel, numeric loopback binding, Origin validation, request limits, and existing mutation approval. Bearer authentication is absent: local processes with socket access can inspect exposed data and propose actions. Origin validation protects a browser boundary, not local-process identity. Do not extend this unauthenticated design to remote access.

Revisit the security design when one of these becomes true:

- the server binds beyond loopback;
- a browser or remote service must connect;
- tokens or grants must survive an application restart;
- multiple users or clients require different permissions;
- tools read or write files at caller-supplied paths, or read sensitive account/device data such as camera frames;
- tools upload to a printer or begin a physical print;
- unattended or remembered approvals expand, including the computation-only exemption and any monitoring policy that authorizes automatic pausing; or
- real usage makes forensic activity history a product requirement.

At that point evaluate authenticated pairing, durable credential storage, per-client grants, tool scopes, TLS/remote policy, revocation, rate controls, privacy review, and a dedicated audit log. Add them in response to the concrete exposure; do not prebuild an enterprise control plane for local v1.

Tier 1 of the candidate catalog trips three of these triggers on its own: `print_send` begins a physical print, `export_file` writes to a caller-supplied path, and `slice_start` and `plan_set` use the computation-only exemption. That review is therefore a gate on Tier 1, not a later concern. Its minimum outcome for a loopback-only v1 is a written answer to each tripped trigger and the per-call approval evidence for every path and printer tool.

## Verification commands and limits of current evidence

From the repository root on the existing macOS development build:

```sh
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target OrcaSlicer agent_bridge_tests shell_integration_harness -- -j6
build/arm64/tests/agent/RelWithDebInfo/agent_bridge_tests.app/Contents/MacOS/agent_bridge_tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp -v
npm --prefix src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI test
build/arm64/tests/shell/RelWithDebInfo/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --mcp-bridge
```

Also run the shell harness with `--mcp` for direct HTTP, `--mcp-setup` for the isolated setup-command fixtures, no argument for normal shell regression, and `--stock` for stock behavior. `--manual-mcp <dedicated-temporary-directory>` provides a disposable two-plate fixture for real clients; do not use the user's normal data directory. Linux helper/launcher checks are documented in [the test README](../../tests/mcp/linux/README.md).

Executed evidence includes native read/visible approval/rejection/Undo/staleness/cancellation/shutdown checks; real Claude Code and Codex CLI reads, rejection, approval, changed-port restart and offline errors using session-only configuration; and Linux ARM64 container tests of the production helper and a compressed AppImage transport fixture. Those Linux tests are not a full GUI release image. A macOS Quit attempt during a setup fixture retained the monitor and later reaped the timed-out children; that does not prove forced OS shutdown behavior.

Still unverified: persistent one-click writes against real client installations; desktop-client read/approve/reject/restart/offline workflows (including local Cowork availability); complete Windows/Linux release packages; macOS universal signing/notarization; and remaining DPI/live-theme checks. The development macOS bundle failed strict signature verification, and the existing CI signing step is restricted to the upstream OrcaSlicer repository. Do not equate a successful local CLI test, a packaging rule, or the presence of signing identities with passing these gates.

## Definition of done

A new tool is done when:

- it fixes a named eval failure;
- its scope and authority are honest;
- the registry is the only definition source;
- the coordinator owns policy and lifecycle;
- the real operation uses Orca's current owner on the GUI thread;
- results and errors are structured and bounded;
- mutation history, approval, staleness, events, and cancellation behave as documented;
- fake, real-adapter, adapter, protocol, and shell evidence pass as applicable;
- no unrelated Orca behavior changes when the JusPrin feature is disabled; and
- the PR records any upstream seam and its rebase evidence.

Tool count is not the success metric. A compact catalog that reliably completes real printing tasks is.

### Printer tests without hardware

Bambu paths (printer-menu Idle / Printing / Offline, Select Machine, print job)
are exercised by an in-process fake that substitutes for the Bambu printer
agent while a real Bambu Lab **system** preset stays selected. How to turn it
on, the JSON control file, isolated-instance rules for agents, and acceptance
checks: [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md).

The Klipper/Moonraker network simulator lives on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`
under `tests/printer_sim/` and covers print-host paths. Do not add a fake
Bambu network layer (MQTT/FTPS/discovery) without an explicit request.

### Platform matrix

Before release completion, cover:

- Windows with WebView2;
- macOS with WKWebView;
- Linux/X11 and supported Wayland configurations with WebKitGTK;
- supported CPU architectures and a physical GPU where applicable;
- 100%, 150%, and 200% scaling or equivalent platform DPI settings;
- light and dark mode;
- keyboard focus, global shortcuts, clipboard, text selection, and IME composition;
- WebView startup, local resource loading, reload, and recovery;
- streaming scroll anchoring while orbiting and resizing;
- idle and streaming CPU/memory observations.

Classify localized CSS, focus, packaging, or backend problems as platform defects unless evidence shows they require a different architecture.

### Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU

A Windows machine with no graphics driver reports system GL 1.1, so the launcher
(`src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp`) loads `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` instead.
Nothing in CMake or this repository supplies that file or what it depends on, so
provision every freshly configured build tree with
`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1`.
Placement is not interchangeable:

| file | goes | because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `opengl32.dll` | `mesa\` subfolder | the launcher loads it by that path; beside the executable it shadows the system GL and the app dies at launch |
| `libgallium_wgl.dll` | beside the executable | the `opengl32.dll` stub imports it, and Windows resolves imports against the process directory |
| `dxil.dll` | beside the executable | Mesa's `d3d12` driver signs translated shaders with it; Windows Server does not ship it, Windows SDKs carry it under `Redist\D3D\x64` |

Each gap has its own silent signature:

- **No `libgallium_wgl.dll`:** GL falls back to 1.1, the log has `glcontext not ready, postpone init` and no `got opengl version` line, and the canvas stays black for the whole session — the retry after a postponed init exists only on Linux.
- **No `dxil.dll`:** GL initializes through `d3d12`, then the process exits with `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw, with no log line, no dialog, and no event-log entry. `slow_bootup` only moves this crash from startup to the first canvas paint.

Confirm what actually loaded from the process's module list rather than from
file presence. The log names the live driver: `4.6 … llvmpipe` is Mesa's software
rasterizer, `4.2 … D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` is Mesa's `d3d12`
driver on WARP. A fully provisioned tree renders under both;
`GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` selects the former.

## Implementation evidence record

For every production area, record:

- product requirement and underlying technical nature;
- current Orca command owner, snapshot location, and event source;
- mature precedents and what each proves;
- remaining delta and risk category;
- production and upstream-owned files touched;
- verification command and exit condition;
- platforms exercised and gaps remaining;
- regression checks for the original Orca path;
- any behavior that could not be tested and why.

## Rebase evidence

The rules for changing upstream-owned files are in [fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). This section states only what a change must produce as evidence.

A change that touches an upstream-owned file is not finished until the handback or pull request records three things:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result**, run against current upstream with both endpoint commits named. For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy resolution is a defect to fix before the change lands, not a note for the person who rebases.
2. **Every upstream line deleted or rewritten**, with where the logic went and why an additive form was not possible.
3. **What the fork now owns** — product policy, a small neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It never proves that a future rebase will merge, and never proves that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the contract tests, the full native build, the multi-plate Prepare/Check workflow, native gizmo input, and the original-Orca regression checks.

The incidents that produced these rules are in [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). Historical logs and spike procedures are in [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

I pulled (already up to date on `jusprin-newui`, clean) and read the handoff, the guide it defers to, and the code it points at. Here's the honest answer.

## What's solid

- **The documents are coherent and the pointers are real.** [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md](agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) has every section the handoff cites, including the normalizer hazard table, the test matrix, and the candidate catalog. The 32-tool journey is exactly the guide's 38 minus `machine`, `calibration`, and `preflight_check`/`print_send`. [ProjectStateDocument.hpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectStateDocument.hpp), [ProjectState.hpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectState.hpp), [FakeWorkspace.hpp](tests/jusprin_support/FakeWorkspace.hpp), [OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp) all exist as described.
- **The M0 claims check out.** [McpProtocol.cpp:208](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp:208) does emit `outputSchema` for every tool, and `validate_output` ([ToolRegistry.cpp:364](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp:364)) really does lack `enum`/`maxLength`.
- **The build tree here works.** Windows Release build from 2026-09-13, Mesa provisioned in both `build/src/Release` and `build/tests/shell/Release`, `claude` CLI 2.1.236 present for the MCP-client transcripts, network to npm/nodejs reachable.
- **I reproduced the measurement baseline.** The macOS recipe doesn't run here (no `python3`), but a PowerShell equivalent against `build/src/Release/jusprin-mcp.exe` gives **9,723 bytes across 5 tools** — the handoff's exact number. So the deferral evidence the PRs must report is measurable on this machine.

## What's missing — and one of it blocks today

**1. Node/npm is not installed. This is a hard blocker, not a nuisance.** Two ways it bites: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Web/CMakeLists.txt:12` is a `FATAL_ERROR` when npm is absent, and adding source files triggers a reconfigure — so the first new tool file breaks the build tree. And the bundles are already gone: there is no `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html` anywhere. I ran the shell harness to check, and it fails exactly there:

```
HARNESS CHECK canvas_renders_fixture PASS
HARNESS CHECK shell_agent_webview_created FAIL
HARNESS ERROR shell: the Agent page did not complete its handshake
```

GL, canvas, plates, selection all pass; the Agent panel doesn't exist on this machine right now. No Agent panel means no approval cards, no in-app eval, no real-adapter evidence for any tool. Fixable without admin — unzip Node per-user and put it on PATH — but I want your go-ahead before installing a toolchain on your box.

**2. No OpenAI key.** The handoff says live calls are required and that the key comes from AppConfig; in fact the live regression is the shell harness `--live-agent` mode ([shell_harness.cpp:3556](tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp:3556)), and it reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment. Nothing is set here and `JusPrin2.conf` has no key. Without it I can deliver every layer of the test matrix except the eval transcripts and the input/cached-token numbers — which are precisely the evidence each milestone PR is required to report.

**3. Two decisions are yours, per the handoff's own open list**: whether `project_attachment_read` and `view_render` ship in M6, and how far the M4 allowlist goes (speed keys or not).

## Three handoff details I'd correct before starting

- The `grep -rn -i live tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp` lead finds nothing — that file has no live test. The live multi-tool regression is [shell_harness.cpp:2033](tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp:2033) onward.
- `kInvalidatingReasons` ([ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:22](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:22)) is a `WorkspaceChangeReasons` mask, a different enum from `ProjectStateChangeReason`. The new reasons need to land in both and in the mapping at [OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:53](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:53). I'd just do both, but the text as written points at one enum.
- The catalog-size recipe is macOS-path-and-`python3`-only. I'll add the Windows equivalent to the guide when I touch it.

## The scope question

M0 through M7 is 32 tools, each owing a real-adapter implementation, an eight-layer test matrix, an eval transcript, and rebase evidence for the upstream seams — the settings work alone, four tools over one preset, was its own multi-week effort with its own handoff. The handoff itself forbids starting a milestone before the previous one's real-adapter tests pass, so this is a sequence of PRs, not one task I can finish in a sitting. My plan would be **M0 + M1 as the first PR**, stopping for your review before M2.

So: give me a yes on installing Node per-user, an `OPENAI_API_KEY` (or an explicit waiver that I ship milestones with the eval line marked unverified), and answers on the two open items — and I have everything else I need to start on M0.
install node and start on M0. when you need openai key, let me know how I can give you. spin up subagent to speed up process as you see fit

**Why:** This looks exactly like an application bug — gestures appear to have no effect and screenshots fail — so it can burn a long time before you realise the session, not the code, is the problem.

- Check `query session` first when input or capture stops working.
- Real UI testing still works without a desktop: `SendMessageTimeout` WM_LBUTTONDOWN / WM_MOUSEMOVE / WM_LBUTTONUP / WM_LBUTTONDBLCLK straight to the child HWND. - A faithful drag must hold the pointer at a fixed **screen** x and recompute the client x from the target window's live `GetWindowRect` each step. Holding client x fixed makes a moving splitter run away, because the app converts with `ClientToScreen` against the window's current position.
- Read results from `EnumChildWindows` + `GetWindowRect` rather than pixels; assert that sibling columns tile the client rect exactly, which catches overlaps a per-window size check cannot see.
- P/Invoke `GetWindowTextW` must be declared `CharSet=CharSet.Unicode`, or the StringBuilder is marshalled as ANSI and the W call overruns the buffer and crashes PowerShell.

The existing setup wizard’s enormous lists of printer and filament profiles should become hardware discovery followed by a short confirmation.

---

## 2.3 Print intent

This surface answers: **What outcome does the user want?**

Instead of beginning with hundreds of process parameters, the product should ask for meaningful requirements.

### What should remain

- Intended use
- Visual versus functional priority
- Strength direction
- Accuracy requirements
- Important dimensions or clearances
- Heat, chemical, outdoor, food-contact, or flexibility requirements
- Desired surface quality
- Maximum acceptable print time
- Material or color requirements
- Acceptable and unacceptable support contact
- Whether this is a prototype or final part

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

The same model can legitimately be printed with different orientations, materials, wall structures, infill, supports, and tolerances depending on its purpose.

A decorative prototype and a load-bearing final component may use identical geometry but require completely different plans.

### What the agent should do

Translate intent into technical settings. For example:

> “This is a visible decorative object, so I oriented it to protect the front surface, moved the seam to the rear, and accepted a longer print to reduce visible layer artifacts.”

The user should judge that reasoning without having to configure every underlying value.

The full intent editor should appear during project creation, import, or when requirements are incomplete. Afterward, Prepare should retain only a compact editable summary. Specialized questions such as food contact, flexibility, critical clearances, and protected support surfaces should appear contextually rather than in every project.

Declare the computation-only approval exemption in the registry

A mutation whose only effect is computation, a replaced computed result, or
the agent's own statement should not cost an approval card; if it does, every
"check this print" spends one and the card stops meaning anything. The
exemption is declared beside the action class, on the definition, so the
registry stays the one place policy is decided. A destructive action never
qualifies, whatever it declares.

Three places had read "requires approval" as a synonym for "is a mutation",
which the exemption would have quietly broken:

- the coordinator's execution-time staleness recheck, which would have left an
  exempt mutation with no staleness protection at all, since an auto-started
  action is never Pending for the eager invalidation to catch;
- the MCP server's streaming decision, which would have dropped progress
  streaming from the calls that take longest; and
- the runtime's progress notifications, suppressed entirely for a call with no
  card. Progress now says "Starting in JusPrin" where an approval-gated call
  says "Awaiting approval in JusPrin".

Each now asks the action class directly, which is the same answer as today for
every shipped tool: no tool declares the exemption yet, and a test pins that.
The coordinator's no-card tests arrive with slice_start, plan_set, and
activity_cancel in M1, since a test cannot supply its own catalog -- the
registry's constructor is private and its definitions are const, and adding a
seam for tests alone was not worth it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

input.new_string: - **Revision.** Every write announces itself so readers refresh. Which announcement, and whether it invalidates pending proposals, is **open** and belongs to the milestone that lands the first writer. The obvious reading — publish a `WorkspaceChangeReasons` bit and add it to `kInvalidatingReasons` — is not implementable as stated: `settings_apply_patch` compares its caller's `expectedRevision` against the current revision for exact equality, so any revision advance between a client's preview and its apply fails as `stale_workspace`. An agent that records its plan between previewing and applying would break its own call. The edit feed (`WorkspaceEditHub`) is the precedent for a feed that reports a change without advancing the revision. Decide per kind: a region annotation generates Orca artifacts and is a real project change; an intent answer or a plan statement is not.

No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. Interim status while the harness rebuild finishes (it's recompiling the GUI library because I touched two widely-included headers).

**Environment unblocked.** Node 24.21.0 is installed per-user and on the user PATH, so CMake's `find_program(npm)` succeeds and the tree configures again. Both web bundles build (`resources/jusprin/{agent,home}/index.html`, 468 KB / 239 KB). The AgentUI suite passes: 131 tests, 10 files. Worth recording: `C:\tools\node` already existed but was on nobody's PATH, which is why it looked missing — that's now fixed in my notes for this machine.

**M0, three of five items done and committed** on `claude/journey-tools-m0`:

- [`b1576f9fc9`](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp) — `validate_output` now accepts `enum` and `maxLength`. `enum` is checked before the type dispatch; `maxLength` counts UTF-8 bytes, matching every other bound the registry states.
- [`51d5901f1c`](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp) — output schemas off the MCP wire. Measured on the same build, before and after: **9,723 → 3,141 bytes for five tools, ~2,430 → ~785 tokens.** Results are still validated internally on every MCP success. I also found the Python bridge test asserting six tools where the registry has had five since the print-review flow was removed, and fixed it — flagged below.
- [`af49a218d7`](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecution.hpp) — the computation-only exemption, declared on the definition beside the action class. Three places treated "requires approval" as a synonym for "is a mutation", and the exemption would have broken all three quietly: the coordinator's execution-time staleness recheck (an auto-started action is never `Pending`, so it would have had *no* staleness protection), the MCP streaming decision, and MCP progress notifications. Each now asks the action class, which is the same answer as today for every shipped tool.

Full agent suite green: 2696 assertions, 168 cases.

**Two things I need from you.**

1. **The OpenAI key.** M0's unit layers don't need it, but M1's eval and the per-request token/cache numbers do, and so does the live agent path in the shell harness. The harness reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment (`shell_harness.cpp:3556`) — not AppConfig, as the handoff says. Easiest: set it as a user environment variable on this box (`setx OPENAI_API_KEY sk-…` in your own terminal, or paste it into the Terminal panel and I'll pick it up from a fresh shell without it ever entering the transcript). I won't put a key in source or fixtures either way.

2. **A decision that M0 surfaced and can't resolve by itself.** The handoff says JusPrin-owned writes publish a change reason and go into `kInvalidatingReasons`. That isn't implementable as written: `settings_apply_patch` compares its caller's `expectedRevision` to the current revision for *exact equality*, so any revision advance between a client's preview and its apply fails as `stale_workspace`. An agent that records its plan between previewing and applying would break its own call. My read: regions genuinely change the model and should invalidate; an intent answer or a plan statement should announce itself without advancing the revision (the edit feed is the existing precedent for exactly that). I've written the question into the guide rather than silently picking, since the first writer lands in M1.

Two smaller notes: I scoped M0's stores to **intent and plan** (both consumed by M1) and left regions to M5 and confirmed printer facts to M2, because their record shapes are the geometry handles and printer identity those milestones define — writing them now would be guessing. And the Python bridge tests can't run here at all: there's no `python3` on this machine. Say the word and I'll install it per-user the way I did Node; until then that one assertion is unverified and the commit message says so.

content.text:
M0 is complete on `claude/journey-tools-m0` — five commits, all fork-owned files, no OrcaSlicer-owned line touched, so there's no rebase evidence to carry.

## The five M0 items

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| Output validator keywords | `enum` + `maxLength`, tested on a definition built in the test rather than a shipped tool |
| Output schemas off the MCP wire | **9,723 → 3,141 bytes** for five tools, ~2,430 → ~785 tokens; `validate_output` still runs on every MCP success |
| Computation-only policy | Declared on the definition; three approval-coupled call sites corrected |
| JusPrin-owned stores | Intent + plan in `state.json`; regions and printer facts deferred to the milestones that define their shapes |
| Fixture retirement plan | Recorded in the guide's catalog record, one fixture per replacement PR |

## Evidence

- `agent_bridge_tests`: **2746 assertions, 171 cases, all passing** (`--order rand --warn NoAssertions`)
- Shell harness, rebuilt from this commit: **292 checks, failures=0, exit 0** — including the Agent panel, which could not even be created before the web bundles existed
- Harness `--mcp-bridge`: **PASS, failures=0**; harness `--mcp`: **PASS, failures=0** — both exercise the live app's real registry catalog
- AgentUI: 131 tests, 10 files
- Catalog bytes measured offline against the same build, before and after

## Three things I could not verify, and why

1. **The Python bridge tests.** No `python3` on this box. I fixed a stale assertion there (it expected six tools; the registry has had five since the print-review flow was removed) and added the `outputSchema`-absence check, but neither has been run. Say the word and I'll install Python per-user like Node.
2. **Live OpenAI evals and per-request token numbers.** Still waiting on the key — see below.
3. **A real Claude Code MCP transcript.** The `claude` CLI on this machine reports "Not logged in", and logging it in with your credentials isn't mine to do. The stdio path is covered by the two harness MCP modes against the live app; the missing dimension is specifically a real third-party client. You can run it in a minute with the fixture: `shell_integration_harness.exe --manual-mcp <dir>`, then point a logged-in Claude Code at `jusprin-mcp --discovery <dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`.

## What I need to start M1

**The OpenAI key**, the way you find easiest:

```bash
setx OPENAI_API_KEY "sk-..."
```

Run that in your own terminal (not through me) and it lands in the user environment; my next shell picks it up without the value ever entering this transcript.

**And the decision I flagged before**, which M1 forces: whether an intent or plan write advances the workspace revision. I've left it written up as open in the guide. My recommendation stands — announce without advancing, because `settings_apply_patch` compares `expectedRevision` for exact equality and an agent recording its plan between preview and apply would fail its own call.

Two smaller calls I made rather than blocking, both stated in the commits: the coordinator's no-card tests land in M1 with `slice_start` and `plan_set` (a test cannot supply its own catalog — the registry's constructor is private and its definitions are `const` — and a test-only seam wasn't worth it), and the stores cover intent and plan only.

Want me to push the branch and open the M0 PR, or hold while you look at the commits locally?

questions.question: When the agent writes down the print intent or its own plan, should that count as a change to the project — the same way moving an object or editing a setting does?

options.label: No, just announce it
options.description: The panel refreshes, but the project revision does not move. Nothing pending gets cancelled. This is what I recommend: settings_apply_patch demands an exact revision match, so if recording a plan bumped the revision, the agent would cancel its own pending settings change just by writing down what it intends to do.
options.preview:
plan_set -> panel refreshes, revision unchanged
settings_apply_patch (pending) -> still valid

options.label: Yes, a real change
options.description: Intent and plan writes bump the revision and cancel anything waiting for approval, exactly as the handoff says. Honest and simple, but the agent must never write a plan while one of its own changes is waiting for you.

options.label: Split it
options.description: Region marks count as real changes (they generate supports, paint, modifiers in the model). Intent and plan only announce themselves. More code, but each kind gets the truthful answer.

questions.question: Should the agent be able to change print speeds in M4, or only the support, adhesion, seam, wall, infill and shell settings the handoff lists?

options.label: Start without, add if needed
options.description: Build the handoff's list, then run the eval. If the agent cannot hit 'under five hours' without speed, that is the evidence for adding speed keys, and I add them in the same milestone. Recommended: every new key costs a full audit of Orca's normalizer, so I would rather pay for the ones the eval proves are needed.

options.label: Include speed now
options.description: Add the speed family up front. Time budget is one of the things people actually ask for, so the agent will reach for it. Costs more audit work in M4 and makes the milestone longer.

options.label: Never speed
options.description: Keep speed a human decision. The agent trades time through layer height, infill and supports only.

questions.question: The tools that return pictures — reading an image you attached, and rendering the plate so the agent can look at it. Both need image plumbing in two adapters first. Ship them in M6, or leave them out of this journey?

options.label: Attachment reading only
options.description: The agent can look at a reference photo or drawing you attached, which is how people actually explain what they want. Rendering the plate waits. Recommended: half the work, most of the value, and the export journey does not need the agent to see the plate.

options.label: Both in M6
options.description: Agent can also render the prepared plate and look at it before slicing. Useful for catching an obviously wrong orientation, but it is the more expensive half and the agent already gets geometry facts as numbers.

options.label: Neither for now
options.description: Finish the model-file-to-G-code journey with no pictures at all, and revisit once it works end to end.

questions.question: When the agent asks what you want from a print, should the questions come from a fixed list, or can it invent its own?

options.label: Fixed list
options.description: The eleven things your product doc names: intended use, looks vs strength, strength direction, accuracy, key dimensions, heat/chemical/outdoor/food/flex needs, surface finish, time limit, material and colour, acceptable support marks, prototype or final. Recommended: a fixed list is what makes 'here is what I still do not know' possible, and keeps two chats recording the same answer the same way.

options.label: Fixed core, free extras
options.description: The eleven are fixed; the agent may add its own named answers for things the list does not cover. More flexible, but the record drifts between chats and the unanswered list gets fuzzy.

options.label: Let it invent
options.description: No fixed vocabulary. Most flexible, least reviewable — and the agent cannot tell you what it still does not know.

input.new_string:
Node is required: the Agent and Home pages are built from TypeScript and their `index.html` is generated, not committed, so a tree without npm fails at configure time and an app built without them shows no Agent panel at all.

The Python bridge tests run there too, with the helper named explicitly, since the default path in `tests/mcp/test_bridge_process.py` is the macOS bundle:

```sh
JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE=build/src/Release/jusprin-mcp.exe python -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp
```

As of 2026-09-16 that reports 8 failures on Windows, all in the live-peer paths — SSE progress, client cancellation, EOF with a pending call, stdout backpressure, the live catalog's header mirroring, and a malformed peer result. They are not caused by any JusPrin change: building the helper from the previous commit reproduces the same 8. The suite had only ever been run on macOS and Linux, so treat them as an unexamined platform gap and do not read a green Windows run into a PR that has not had one.

input.tldr:
While verifying M0 I ran the Python bridge tests on Windows for the first time. Eight of them fail in the live-peer paths, and building the helper from an older commit reproduces the same eight, so it is a platform gap nobody has looked at. A separate session could work out whether the helper misbehaves on Windows or the tests assume POSIX.</tldr>
<parameter name="prompt">In C:\src\JusPrin (branch claude/journey-tools-m0 or later), the Python MCP bridge tests fail on Windows in eight live-peer cases. Investigate and fix whichever side is wrong.

Run them with:
  $env:JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE = "C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release\jusprin-mcp.exe"
  C:\Users\guitest\.local\python-3.13.9\python.exe -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp

Failing as of 2026-09-16:
- test_client_cancellation_and_eof_close_http (both modern=False and True) - KeyError 'method': expected a notifications/progress frame, got something else
- test_progress_and_terminal_sse
- test_cancellation_discards_progress_queued_behind_backpressure
- test_eof_with_pending_call
- test_live_catalog_header_mirroring_and_version_warning
- test_malformed_peer_result_becomes_an_error_not_invalid_stdout
- test_one_process_follows_app_start_stop_and_replacement ('workspace_unavailable' != 'connection_lost')

These are NOT regressions: building jusprin-mcp from commit f797b2cd62 (before the M0 work) reproduces the same eight. The suite had only ever been run on macOS and Linux (see tests/mcp/linux/run.sh and the verification section of agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md).

The question to answer: does the stdio bridge (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/Bridge/) genuinely behave differently on Windows - non-blocking stdio, select() on pipes, SSE framing, process teardown - or do the tests assume POSIX semantics the helper is right to not provide? Fix the side that is wrong, keep the macOS/Linux runs green, and record the finding in the guide's verification section, which currently documents the failures as an unexamined platform gap.

Let the agent record what the print is for, and its plan

Two tools over the M0 store, and the first sections on workspace_inspect.

intent_update takes named answers the agent chooses rather than a fixed
questionnaire: field names are its own. That is a deliberate product choice,
and it costs the derived "what do I still not know" list, so the tool buys it
back -- an entry with a question and no value is something asked and
unanswered, and those come back as openQuestions. The card is where the user
confirms the agent understood them, so it shows the interpreted answer rather
than field names, and an answer approved there becomes user_confirmed unless
the agent marks it assumed. Nothing is written before approval.

plan_set replaces the whole plan, because a plan is one statement and not a
log, and it is the first tool to claim the computation-only exemption: it
records only the agent's own words, so it runs with no card.

Neither advances the workspace revision. settings_apply_patch compares its
caller's expectedRevision for exact equality, so an agent that recorded its
plan between previewing a settings change and applying it would otherwise
cancel its own call.

workspace_inspect gains sections. A caller that sends none gets exactly what
it got before, and the summary's fields leave the output schema's required
list so a caller that asks only for intent is not handed a project summary it
did not want. It also stops being a strict OpenAI function: strict mode cannot
express an optional argument.

Start Orca's slicing run from a tool, and read it back

slice_start posts Orca's own toolbar events after selecting the plate, which
is exactly what the fork's header button does. That keeps one owner for
slicing: the slice-all bookkeeping, the Prepare switch, and the auto-preview
rule all travel with those events, and no OrcaSlicer-owned line changes.

The call returns when the run has started, not when it ends. Waiting would
mean a second job engine; instead the handle it returns names the run, and
workspace_inspect's new slicing section reports what the slicer is doing and
what each plate currently holds. Running is a property of the workspace rather
than of a plate, because one background process serves the whole application.

Two refusals worth stating. Nothing in Orca records who started a run, so a
slice already in flight may be the person's: a second start is refused unless
the caller passes preempt, and preempt brings back the approval card that
slicing is otherwise exempt from. That is the first argument-sensitive
approval decision, so it lives in the registry beside the other two.

input.command:
cd /c/src/JusPrin && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Report what a sliced plate says about itself

slice_report reads the plate's own Print and GCodeProcessorResult, the same
owners the preview legend reads, so a report can never disagree with the
numbers on screen. Three sections: summary is time and per-filament length,
weight and cost; findings are Orca's warnings and errors with the object each
belongs to, its conflict string, and whether a toolpath leaves the bed;
material is filament and tool changes with the volume purged for them.

Four things the sources make necessary rather than optional:

Warnings live per milestone step, on the print and on each object, not in one
list, and invalidating a step leaves its warnings behind marked stale. The
report walks both sets and keeps only the current ones. Orca's plate-level
warnings come through its own words for them, and the ones it deliberately has
no words for are dropped rather than shown as a sentinel.

The result's toolpath_outside flag is only ever written by a 3mf, so on a
plate just sliced it is stale. The report asks the build volume instead, the
way the canvas does before drawing the same warning.

Cost is the cost of the whole print or it is not shown, the rule the setup
card already applies: one unpriced spool makes the total a lie.

A plate that has not been sliced, or whose slice is being replaced, reports
valid:false and no summary at all. Zeros would read as a print that takes no
time and costs nothing.

Findings are ordered critical first so a bounded list loses the mildest
findings, never the ones that stop the print.

Catalog after: MCP 9 definitions and 6,915 bytes, in-app 11 and 6,482.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

input.old_string: Only `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, `settings_get`, `settings_preview_patch`, and `settings_apply_patch` are MCP-visible.
input.new_string:
`workspace_inspect` takes an optional `sections` list — `summary` (the default, and exactly what it returned before sections existed), `intent`, `plan`, `slicing`. Its output schema requires only the identity fields, so a caller that asks for one section is not handed the rest. It is no longer a strict OpenAI function: strict mode cannot express an optional argument.

Intent and plan writes do not advance the workspace revision, and that is deliberate — see [JusPrin-owned project state](#jusprin-owned-project-state). The intent vocabulary is the agent's own; an entry carrying a question and no value is what it asked and does not know, which is where `openQuestions` comes from.

`slice_start` posts Orca's own `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` / `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_ALL` after selecting the plate, the way the fork's header button does, so the slice-all bookkeeping and the auto-preview rule stay with their owner and no upstream line changes. It returns when the run starts, and the result is read from the `slicing` section. Nothing in Orca records who started a run, so a second start is refused unless `preempt` is passed, and `preempt` is the catalog's one argument-sensitive approval decision.

Only `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, `settings_get`, `settings_preview_patch`, `settings_apply_patch`, `intent_update`, `plan_set`, `slice_start`, and `slice_report` are MCP-visible.

content.text:
M1's five tools are done and committed; the app is rebuilding so I can verify the real adapter with the new catalog. Status:

## M1 (13 commits on the branch, 5 for M1)

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `intent_update` | Records what the print is for, in the agent's own field names; a question with no value becomes an open question |
| `plan_set` | Replaces the whole plan; first tool to use the computation-only exemption |
| `slice_start` | Posts Orca's own toolbar slice events; returns a handle, refuses to preempt without saying so |
| `slice_report` | Time, per-filament length/weight/cost, Orca's warnings with their object, conflicts, bed check, material changes |
| `workspace_inspect` | Now takes `sections`: summary, intent, plan, slicing |

**178 test cases, 2,916 assertions, all passing.** Catalog grew 5 → 9 MCP definitions (3,147 → 6,905 bytes, ~1,726 tokens).

Three decisions you made are now in the code: plan writes don't move the revision (so an agent can't cancel its own pending settings change); intent fields are free-form, with open questions recorded explicitly since nothing can derive them; `preempt` on `slice_start` is the one argument-sensitive approval decision.

## One thing I got wrong and caught

The shell harness binary I ran earlier was **stale** — it carried the pre-M1 catalog, so that "292 checks, failures=0" proved the app still works, not that M1's tools work in it. I found it when a live MCP `tools/list` against the running app returned the old five names. Rebuilding now; the real-adapter verification and the MCP eval are pending that, and I won't call M1 verified until both run against a binary built from HEAD.

Also fixed: the catalog measurement recipe silently reported **zero tools** once M1's schemas nested deeper than PowerShell's default conversion depth. Not an error — a zero, in the number every milestone PR rests on. Both conversions now carry `-Depth`, and the guide says why.

Still outstanding for M1: the live MCP transcript (script is written and waiting on the build), fresh OpenAI token/cache numbers with 11 in-app definitions, and the "edit a setting in the GUI, see it go stale" half of the eval, which needs a click I can't make headlessly.

content.text:
M1 is done and verified end to end. Here's where things stand.

## M1 complete — 10 commits, 5 tools

**Every layer green, all on a binary built from HEAD** (after I caught and fixed the stale-binary problem):

| Layer | Result |
|---|---|
| Registry, decoder, coordinator, fake, results | 178 cases, 2,916 assertions |
| Real adapter + shell | 292 checks, failures=0 |
| MCP stdio bridge / direct HTTP | failures=0 each |
| Live MCP eval | real Orca numbers, below |
| Live OpenAI | failures=0, 11 in-app definitions |

**The M1 eval, run against the live app by an external MCP client:**

```
== slice ==   handle=t-8 started=True running=True
== report ==  print time: 16 min (978 s)
              filament:   3.94 g, 1.3 m, cost known: True
              findings:   0   (conflict: '', outside bed: False)
```

`slice_start` streamed its reply over SSE and took **no approval card** — the computation-only policy from M0 working through a real external client, which is the thing that policy existed for.

## What the token numbers say about deferral

| | first request of a chat | later requests |
|---|---|---|
| M0 (7 in-app defs) | 803 tokens, 0 cached | 77–86% cached |
| M1 (11 in-app defs) | 1,733 tokens, 0 cached | up to 92% cached (5,376 / 5,864) |

Four definitions cost **~930 tokens once per conversation**, and roughly nothing after the first request. So the deferral trigger isn't definition count — it's the first request of each conversation becoming expensive on its own, or transcripts showing wrong-tool selection. Both are now written into the guide as the things to watch.

## Two bugs my own verification caught

The harness binary I first ran was stale and carried the pre-M1 catalog — the "PASS" it produced was real but proved nothing about M1. And the catalog measurement recipe reported **zero tools** under Windows PowerShell 5.1, which can't parse schemas this deep and says so by returning nothing. Both are fixed, and the guide now names `pwsh` explicitly, because a silent zero in the number every milestone PR rests on is worth a sentence.

One M1 item I could not automate: the "edit a setting in the GUI, then ask again and see the slice go stale" half of the eval needs a click in the running app. The `invalidatedBy` path it exercises is covered by fake-workspace tests, but not live.

M2 has started — I'm tracing the preset and device owners for `presets_list` and `printer_list`, the two read-only setup tools that need no dialog suppression.

<result>## 1. `presets_list` — PresetBundle / PresetCollection

### The three collections and how to enumerate

`C:\src\JusPrin\src\libslic3r\PresetBundle.hpp:314-321`

```cpp
    PresetCollection            prints;
    PresetCollection            sla_prints;
    PresetCollection            filaments;
    PresetCollection            sla_materials;
    PrinterPresetCollection     printers;
    PhysicalPrinterCollection   physical_printers;
```

Instance: `wxGetApp().preset_bundle` (`GUI_App`), used exactly that way in the fork at `SetupCommands.cpp:58`, `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:248`, `OrcaHomeBackend.cpp:179`.

Iteration: `PresetCollection` exposes `begin()/end()` that **skip the default presets**:

`C:\src\JusPrin\src\libslic3r\Preset.hpp:503-508`
```cpp
    Iterator        begin() { return m_presets.begin() + m_num_default_presets; }
    ConstIterator   begin() const { return m_presets.cbegin() + m_num_default_presets; }
    ...
    Iterator        lbegin() { return m_presets.begin(); }          // :499 — includes defaults
```

`m_num_default_presets` is 1 per collection (`PresetCollection::PresetCollection` calls `add_default_preset` once — `Preset.cpp:1497-1507`; the only other `add_default_preset` in `PresetBundle.cpp` is commented out at `:367`). `const std::deque<Preset>& get_presets() const` (`Preset.hpp:666`) and `operator()()` (`:525`) give the raw deque including defaults.

**Important subtlety:** range-for over a collection yields `m_presets[i]`, i.e. the *stored* preset, never `m_edited_preset`. The index-based accessor is the one that substitutes the edited copy:

`Preset.hpp:675-679`
```cpp
    Preset&         preset(size_t idx, bool real = false) {
        if (real) return m_presets[idx];
        return (idx == m_idx_selected) ? m_edited_preset : m_presets[idx];
    }
```

So for the selected preset, an iterated `Preset&` carries the *saved* config and `is_dirty` as maintained by `update_dirty()`, not the user's in-flight edits.

### Visible vs hidden

`Preset.hpp:234-237`
```cpp
    // Preset is visible, if it is associated with a printer model / variant that is enabled in the AppConfig
    // or if it has no printer model / variant association.
    // Also the "default" preset is only visible, if it is the only preset in the list.
    bool                is_visible  = true;
```

Set by `Preset::set_visible_from_appconfig` (`Preset.cpp:853-882`), called from `PresetBundle.cpp:2473, 2598, 2622`. Behaviour per type:
- `vendor == nullptr` → returns immediately, so **user presets keep `is_visible = true`** (`Preset.cpp:857`).
- `TYPE_PRINTER` → `app_config.get_variant(vendor->id, model, variant)` — i.e. "is this vendor/model/nozzle installed" (`:864`).
- `TYPE_FILAMENT` / `TYPE_SLA_MATERIAL` → membership in AppConfig's `SECTION_FILAMENTS` (`:865-878`), also checking `renamed_from`.
- `TYPE_PRINT` (process) falls through both branches → **process presets are never hidden by this path**. Filtering a process list is `is_compatible` only.

Default-preset visibility is separately toggled by `set_default_suppressed` (`Preset.cpp:3330-3338`) and by `update_compatible_internal` (`Preset.cpp:3375-3381`).

`num_visible()` at `Preset.hpp:766` counts over the whole deque including defaults.

Orca also carries `Preset::m_excluded_from` (`Preset.hpp:275`), used only inside `is_compatible_with_printer` for OrcaFilamentLibrary presets — not a separate visibility flag.

### Per-preset fields

All public, `Preset.hpp:224-296`:

| field | line | note |
|---|---|---|
| `Type type` | 224 | `TYPE_PRINT`/`TYPE_FILAMENT`/`TYPE_PRINTER` (`:206-222`) |
| `bool is_default` | 228 | the `- default -` entry |
| `bool is_external` | 231 | loaded but not imported (3mf/gcode-embedded) |
| `bool is_system` | 233 | read-only vendor profile |
| `bool is_visible` | 237 | see above |
| `bool is_dirty` | 239 | see "selected vs edited" below |
| `bool is_compatible` | 241 | see below |
| `bool is_project_embedded` | 244 | |
| `std::string name` | 251 | |
| `std::string file` | 255 | |
| `const VendorProfile *vendor` | 257 | **null for user presets**; `vendor->name` / `vendor->id` (`Preset.hpp:123-124`) |
| `std::string alias` | 266 | |
| `std::vector<std::string> renamed_from` | 270 | |
| `std::string bundle_id` | 282 | fork addition |
| `std::string setting_id`, `filament_id`, `user_id`, `base_id`, `sync_info`, `description`, `updated_time` | 288-294 | cloud sync metadata |

Derived predicates:
```cpp
    bool  is_user() const { return ! this->is_default && ! this->is_system && ! this->is_project_embedded && ! this->is_from_bundle(); }   // :246
    bool  is_from_bundle() const { return ! bundle_id.empty(); }                                                                           // :283
    std::string get_printer_id() const { return vendor ? vendor->id : ""; }                                                                // :380
    std::string label(bool no_alias) const;   // :311 — prepends "(modified)" when is_dirty (impl Preset.cpp:765-769)
```

`inherits()` is **not a member string** — it is a config option accessor:
```cpp
    static std::string& inherits(DynamicPrintConfig &cfg) { return cfg.option<ConfigOptionString>("inherits", true)->value; }  // :319
    const std::string&  inherits() const { return Preset::inherits(const_cast<Preset*>(this)->config); }                       // :321
```
Note the `true` — **create-if-missing**. See the mutation section.

**Vendor caveat the fork already documented:** `Preset::vendor` names the *profile bundle*, not the brand. `SetupCommands.hpp:41-46`:

> `// The filament's brand -- "Bambu Lab", "eSUN", "Generic" -- read from the preset's own filament_vendor option. Not Preset::vendor, which names the profile bundle the preset shipped in ("BBL", "OrcaFilamentLibrary") and so can never identify an unbranded preset.`

and the implementation `SetupCommands.cpp:45-51` maps the sentinel `"(Undefined)"` to empty.

### Compatibility with the current printer

`is_compatible` is a **cached flag**, not computed on read. It is written only by `PresetCollection::update_compatible_internal` (`Preset.cpp:3340-3385`), reached through `PresetCollection::update_compatible` (`Preset.hpp:755-764`) and `PresetBundle::update_compatible` (`PresetBundle.cpp:5300`). Callers are all GUI/selection-change sites (`Tab.cpp:1459, 5034, 6202, 6741`, `MainFrame.cpp:3764`, `GUI_App.cpp:7177`, `PresetBundle.cpp:542, 811, 826, 1060`).

The rule itself, `Preset.cpp:809-841`:
```cpp
bool is_compatible_with_printer(const PresetWithVendorProfile &preset, const PresetWithVendorProfile &active_printer, const DynamicPrintConfig *extra_config)
{
    // Orca: check excluded printers
    if (preset.vendor != nullptr && preset.preset.type == Preset::TYPE_FILAMENT) { ... m_excluded_from ... }
    auto &condition               = preset.preset.compatible_printers_condition();
    auto *compatible_printers     = dynamic_cast<const ConfigOptionStrings*>(preset.preset.config.option("compatible_printers"));
    bool  has_compatible_printers = compatible_printers != nullptr && ! compatible_printers->values.empty();
    if (! has_compatible_printers && ! condition.empty()) {
        try { return PlaceholderParser::evaluate_boolean_expression(condition, active_printer.preset.config, extra_config); }
        catch (const std::runtime_error &err) { ...; return true; }   // parse error ⇒ "compatible with everything"
    }
    return preset.preset.is_default || active_printer.preset.name.empty() || !has_compatible_printers ||
           std::find(...) != compatible_printers->values.end() ||
           (!active_printer.preset.is_system && is_compatible_with_parent_printer(preset, active_printer));
}
```

Two mechanisms, in priority order: the `compatible_printers` **list** of printer preset names wins; only when that list is absent/empty is the `compatible_printers_condition` **expression** evaluated.

### Can enumeration or compatibility evaluation mutate?

Yes, in three distinct ways. In decreasing severity:

1. **`PresetCollection::update_compatible(...)` selects a different preset.** `Preset.hpp:755-762`:
   ```cpp
       if (this->update_compatible_internal(...) == (size_t)-1) {
           size_t index = this->first_compatible_idx(prefered_condition);
           this->select_preset(index);
       }
   ```
   and `update_compatible_internal` itself clears the selection (`Preset.cpp:3365-3370`), writes `is_compatible` on every preset (`:3360, 3372`), and flips default-preset `is_visible` (`:3375-3381`). `select_preset` then resets `is_dirty = false` on *every* preset and rebuilds `m_edited_preset` (`Preset.cpp:3573-3579`). **Never call this from a read-only tool.** Read the cached `is_compatible` flag, as `SetupCommands::compatible_filaments` does.

2. **`Preset::compatible_printers_condition()` and `inherits()` insert a config key.** Both use `cfg.option<...>(key, /*create=*/true)` (`Preset.hpp:319, 338, 346`), and `DynamicConfig::optptr(key, true)` inserts a default-constructed option into the map (`Config.cpp:1562-1583`). The `const` overloads `const_cast` their way there (`Preset.hpp:321, 343, 351`). `is_compatible_with_printer` calls `preset.preset.compatible_printers_condition()` at `Preset.cpp:825` — so **evaluating compatibility yourself writes to the preset's `DynamicPrintConfig`**.
   It does not in practice create a spurious dirty: the inserted value is the default (empty string) and `ConfigBase::diff` ignores keys missing from either side (`Config.cpp:518-528`). But it is a non-const write to shared state from a nominally read-only path — relevant if you ever touch presets off the main thread.

3. **`get_selected_preset()` (non-const) can change the selection.** `Preset.hpp:623-629`:
   ```cpp
       Preset&         get_selected_preset() {
           if ((m_idx_selected < 0) || (m_idx_selected >= m_presets.size())) { select_preset(first_visible_idx()); }
   ```
   The `const` overload (`:630`) does not. Hold the bundle as `const PresetBundle*` — as `SetupCommands.cpp:58` and `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:248` do — and this cannot fire.

Safe reads: iterating `begin()/end()` or `get_presets()`, `get_selected_idx()`, `get_selected_preset_name()`, the const `get_selected_preset()`/`get_edited_preset()`, `current_is_dirty()`, `current_dirty_options()`, `get_preset_with_vendor_profile()`, `first_visible_idx()`, `num_visible()`. Not safe: `update_dirty()` (`Preset.hpp:794`, writes flags), `select_preset*`, `update_compatible*`, `set_default_suppressed`, `discard_current_changes`.

Reading a preset does **not** touch the workspace revision. Revision only advances through `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::publish_change` → `Workspace.hpp:440` (`++m_state->revision`); `snapshot()` reads it const at `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:239`.

**`Shell/SetupCommands.cpp:185-209`** — `printer_connection()`, the same ladder for the *selected* machine, with an explicit scope statement worth quoting verbatim:
```cpp
PrinterConnection printer_connection()
{
    PrinterConnection connection;
    // Non-const: use_bbl_network() is not a const member on PresetBundle.
    PresetBundle* presets = wxGetApp().preset_bundle;
    // Only the Bambu network path reports a live machine state. Every other
    // print host is "not connected" here, which is a statement about what
    // JusPrin can observe, not a claim about the machine.
    if (presets == nullptr || !presets->use_bbl_network()) return connection;
    auto* devices = wxGetApp().getDeviceManager();
    if (devices == nullptr) return connection;
    MachineObject* machine = devices->get_selected_machine();
    if (machine == nullptr) return connection;
    connection.monitor_available = true;
    if (!machine->is_connected())      connection.state = ConnectionState::Offline;
    else if (machine->is_in_printing()) connection.state = ConnectionState::Printing;
    else                                connection.state = ConnectionState::Idle;
```
`ConnectionState` enum at `SetupCommands.hpp:88-94`. Note this gates on `use_bbl_network()` — given (b) above, that gate is narrower than the machine list actually is, and would exclude a Moonraker `MachineObject`.

```cpp
// StatusRow.cpp:350-355

// remembers for it. Nothing here writes; a swap goes through SetupCommands.
void StatusRow::refresh_chip()
{
    const auto printer = SetupCommands::current_printer();
    m_chip->set_printer(printer.nickname, printer.valid ? wxString::Format("%g", printer.nozzle) : wxString{});
```
So the chip's nozzle is the **preset's** `nozzle_diameter`, while Home's is the **device-reported** one. Those two can legitimately disagree; `OrcaHomeBackend.cpp:167-168` says so explicitly. Your tool should say which it is reporting.

`SetupCommands.cpp:361-379` (`set_printer_access_code`) is the only other direct `MachineObject` read in the Shell — it uses `devices->get_my_machine(dev_id)` and treats null as "no longer on your network".

- `OrcaHomeBackend::printers()` — method on a `MainFrame&`/`SpoolStore*` holder.
- `StatusRow::*` — a `wxWindow` subclass.
- `PrinterMenu` — explicitly one-printer-only by design (`PrinterMenu.hpp:6-9`: *"Listing several printers, adding one, and connecting a non-Bambu print host are separate work; this slice shows one machine"*).

List the presets this installation actually offers

presets_list pages the printer, filament, and process collections with the
name a selection takes, the label the user sees, the vendor bundle, and
whether each is a system preset, selected, and compatible.

It reports Orca's cached compatibility verdict and never asks for a fresh one.
Asking is not read-only: update_compatible rewrites the flag on every preset,
flips default-preset visibility, and can change the selection outright, and
even evaluating one preset's condition inserts a key into its config. The
fork's own filament listing already made that choice; this follows it rather
than deriving the rule a second time.

Three more things the sources make necessary. Hidden and default presets are
skipped: hidden means this installation does not offer it, and a default is
Orca's placeholder, not something anyone prints with. What a project prints
with is the bundle's per-extruder filament choice, not the filament tab's
selection, so that is what "selected" means for filaments. And the bundle is
held const throughout, because the non-const accessors can select a preset
when the current index is out of range.

The page reports the total it is a page of, so an agent knows to follow the
cursor rather than treating one page as the catalogue.

Also folds the settings module's case-folding helper into one ascii_lower
rather than adding a second one beside it.

Catalog after: MCP 10 definitions and 7,670 bytes, in-app 12 and 7,112.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

List the printers the app knows, including the ones it cannot reach

printer_list reports each machine's activity, the nozzle and materials it last

It extends the fork's own discovery rather than copying it: discover_printers
already snapshots device fields on the GUI thread without letting a

that matters. Setup offers printers you can connect to now, so it hides the
ones the app has not heard from; "what printers do I have" is a different
question, and a printer on the shelf is a real answer to it.

Activity comes from upstream's own is_in_printing, not a list of state names
written out again -- that list has been got wrong here before, and a printer
in PREPARE showed as idle for it. Offline means this application has observed
nothing recently, which is a statement about what it can see and not a claim
about the machine, and the description says so.

Fields the device has not reported are absent rather than zero: a nozzle of
0.0 mm is a claim it never made. The in-process Bambu fake can drive activity
and offline, so those paths are testable without hardware; materials are not,
because the fake announces an empty AMS.

Catalog after: MCP 11 definitions and 8,304 bytes, in-app 13 and 7,630.

content.text:
M2's two read-only setup tools are in. Status while the app rebuilds for real-adapter verification:

## 18 commits on `claude/journey-tools-m0`

**M0** (machinery) and **M1** (the core loop) are complete and verified. **M2** has its first two tools:

| Tool | Notable |
|---|---|
| `presets_list` | Reports Orca's *cached* compatibility verdict and never asks for a fresh one — asking rewrites every preset's flag, flips default visibility, and can change the selection outright |
| `printer_list` | Extends the fork's existing `discover_printers` with one argument rather than copying it; activity comes from upstream's `is_in_printing`, not a re-written list of state names |

**180 test cases, 2,989 assertions, all passing.** Catalog: 11 MCP definitions (8,304 bytes), 13 in-app (7,630).

Two judgment calls worth naming. `presets_list` hides hidden and default presets — hidden means this installation doesn't offer it, and a default is Orca's placeholder, not something anyone prints with. And `printer_list` deliberately *includes* printers the app can't reach, because "what printers do I have" isn't the question setup asks; a printer on the shelf is a real answer, reported as offline with its unreported fields absent rather than zeroed.

The in-process Bambu fake can drive activity and offline states, so those paths are testable without hardware. Materials aren't — the fake announces an empty AMS — and I've said so in the commit rather than implying coverage I don't have.

Still ahead in M2: `printer_setup_preview` and `printer_setup`, then `project_open`/`project_save`/`history_restore`. The project tools are where this stops being additive — they need Orca's load-path dialogs (inch conversion, oversized model, embedded settings) reachable as inputs, which means touching OrcaSlicer-owned files and carrying the rebase evidence fork stewardship requires. That's the first real upstream seam in this journey.

Stopping here with a clean tree. **19 commits on `claude/journey-tools-m0`: M0 and M1 complete and verified, M2 half done.**

## Verified against the live app, not just the fakes

`presets_list` reading real Orca data through MCP:

```
== process presets ==   total=10 truncated=True next='5'
    0.08mm Extra Fine  [Bambulab] system=True
    0.12mm Fine        [Bambulab] system=True
== filaments matching PLA ==   total=6
    Generic PLA          compatible=True
    Bambu PLA Basic      compatible=True
```

Harness: **292 checks, failures=0**, plus `--mcp-bridge` clean. Unit layers: **180 cases, 2,989 assertions**.

`printer_list` returns empty with no device attached — correct, and the only path I proved live. The populated path is covered by unit tests; verifying it for real needs the in-process Bambu fake, which wants a real Bambu *system* preset installed in the fixture datadir and a conf edit that broke on Orca's trailing comment. I stopped rather than spend the session on fixture plumbing, and it's stated that way rather than implied covered.

## What the journey has now

**14 tools**, up from 5. MCP catalog 11 definitions / 8,304 bytes; in-app 13 / 7,630.

M0's machinery, M1's whole core loop (intent, plan, slice, report), and M2's two read-only setup tools. Every commit is one unit of work with its reasoning in the message.

## Where the next session should start

**`printer_setup_preview` is the next piece, and it nearly wasn't possible.** Building `presets_list` turned up that `update_compatible` can't serve a preview — it rewrites the compatibility flag on every preset, flips default-preset visibility, and will *select a different preset* when the current one stops being compatible. The handoff anticipated this and said to drop the preview rather than fake it. It doesn't need dropping: the free `is_compatible_with_printer` takes the printer to evaluate against as an argument, so a candidate can be scored without committing anything. That route, and the one side effect to pin with a test, are now written into the guide's candidate row so it isn't rediscovered.

After that, `project_open` and friends are where this stops being purely additive — Orca's load-path dialogs have to become inputs, which means the first OrcaSlicer-owned edits in this journey and the rebase evidence fork stewardship requires.

Three things remain unverified and are recorded as such: the eight pre-existing Windows failures in the Python bridge tests (a chip is queued for them), a real third-party MCP client transcript (the `claude` CLI here isn't logged in), and the "edit a setting in the GUI, watch the slice go stale" half of M1's eval, which needs a click I can't make headlessly.
